It stood toward the border of Edom in the Negeb.
It is named with Dimonah and Adadah among the far cities.
It witnesses to the LORD’s exact dividing of the land by lot.
usage: Like Kinah at the desert’s edge in the south of Judah, no portion of the saint’s heritage is too far for the care of God.
The LORD who set the south coast toward Edom has determined the bounds of our habitation also.
God keeps His people’s portion even at its furthest and most exposed frontier.

etymology: Hebrew yiphtach, “he openeth” or “God openeth,” a town in the lowland (the Shephelah) of the tribe of Judah.
biblical_def: Iphtah was a town of the lowland, the Shephelah, in the great inheritance of the tribe of Judah. It is named among the cities of that low country, set with Ashnah and Nezib in the roll of Judah’s towns numbered after the conquest of the land (Jos 15:43). The dictionary does not strain after the uncertain points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little lowland town among the goodly heritage He measured out to His people. The portion of Judah was wide and full of cities, yet not one of them was beneath the notice of the God who apportioned the land. The same LORD who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people set also the boundary of Judah and the place of every town within it (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The Hebrew name, signifying “he openeth” and akin to that of Jephthah the judge, may speak of the opening of a way or a spring; and it is a fitting witness, for the same God who opened the land to His people by lot is He who openeth His hand and satisfieth the desire of every living thing. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and Iphtah, a name spoken but once, stood within that pleasant portion as a witness to His exact and faithful dividing.
webster_summary: A town of the lowland of Judah, named once among the cities of the Shephelah.
webster_full: IPHTAH, a town in the lowland or Shephelah of the tribe of Judah.
It is named with Ashnah and Nezib in the roll of Judah’s cities.
The Hebrew name signifies “he openeth” or “God openeth.”
It belonged to the southern allotment given to Judah after the conquest.
It witnesses to the LORD’s exact apportioning of the land by lot.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD’s sovereign apportioning of every saint’s portion.
corruption_paragraphs: Iphtah is a town of the sacred geography, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name in the lowland of Judah may know it for a real place in a real inheritance, given by a real God to a real people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God in the least things and His open hand toward His people. He who set the bounds of Judah and the place of every town within it is the same who has determined the times before appointed and the bounds of every nation and every soul. The saint who feels his portion small or hidden may remember Iphtah, a name spoken but once, yet written for ever in the book of God’s faithful dividing of the land.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “he openeth,” Iphtah names a lowland town of Judah.

etymology: Hebrew yiphtach-’el, “God openeth,” named in “the valley of Jiphthah-el,” which ran along the border between Zebulun and Asher.
biblical_def: Jiphthah-el is named in “the valley of Jiphthah-el,” a valley that marked the border between the tribes of Zebulun and Asher in the northern allotment. The coast of Zebulun reached unto the valley of Jiphthah-el on the north (Jos 19:14), and the border of Asher came round to the same valley toward the side of the land (Jos 19:27), so that this one ravine served as a shared landmark between two tribes. The dictionary does not labour the uncertain points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD set even this little valley to part the inheritance of brethren, that each tribe might know its bounds and keep the ancient landmark its fathers had received (Pro 22:28). The dividing of Zebulun from Asher was no work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). The Hebrew name, signifying “God openeth,” is fitting for a valley that opened a way between the hills and a way between the tribes. The lines were fallen unto Zebulun and unto Asher in pleasant places, and the valley of Jiphthah-el stood between them as a witness that the LORD orders even the borders that distinguish His people one from another, and that brethren may dwell at peace where God has drawn the line.
webster_summary: A valley forming the border between Zebulun and Asher in the northern allotment.
webster_full: JIPHTHAH-EL, a valley marking the border between the tribes of Zebulun and Asher.

The border of Asher came round to the same valley toward the side of the land.
The Hebrew name signifies “God openeth,” fitting for a valley opening a way between the hills.
It witnesses to the LORD’s ordering of the borders that part His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s ordering of the borders that distinguish His people, and the keeping of the ancient landmark. He who set this valley between Zebulun and Asher is the same who has determined the times before appointed and the bounds of every nation and every soul.
